lead: Aircraft wings and fuselages are thin-walled beams, and this unit finds the direct stress and the deflection in them when the bending is not symmetric. After it you can compute section properties for an idealised boom-and-wall section, place the neutral axis for any skew moment, get the deflection direction, and handle a temperature gradient through the depth.
about: This unit treats a thin-walled aircraft beam as a set of walls and stringers carrying direct stress. Chapter 4.1 fixes the sign conventions and the simple σ = My/I result, including the anticlastic curvature it predicts. Chapter 4.2 removes the symmetry condition, adds the product second moment I_xy and locates the tilted neutral axis. Chapter 4.3 turns those stresses into deflections in two planes. Chapter 4.4 justifies replacing a real section by booms plus thin walls and shows how to compute I_xx, I_yy and I_xy from them. Chapter 4.5 applies the idealisation to stringer-stiffened wing boxes under skew loads. Chapter 4.6 closes with thermal gradients, which bend a section exactly as a moment does.

chapters.idea: When the moment acts about a principal axis the stress is σ = M y / I, the beam curves with 1/R = M / EI, and Poisson contraction makes the cross-section curve the other way too.
chapters.depth: Assumptions of simple bending: plane sections stay plane, small deflections, linear elastic material, loads in a plane through a principal axis. Derive σ = M y / I and M = EI / R, define every symbol, give the section modulus Z = I / y_max, and fix one sign convention for sagging and hogging. Draw the stress diagram: zero at the centroidal neutral axis, linear through the depth, largest at the outer fibre. Then anticlastic bending: the stretched fibres contract sideways, so the cross-section curves in its own plane at 1/R′ = ν / R, where ν is Poisson's ratio. The beam becomes saddle-shaped. Flanges and stiffeners resist this, so the effect is much larger on a plain strip than on a wing box.

figure.title: From moment to stress and back-curvature
figure.aria: A top-down chain from the applied moment to the beam curvature, the strain and the direct stress, ending at the transverse anticlastic curvature produced by Poisson contraction.

chapters.example: An aluminium alloy beam has E = 70 GPa, ν = 0.33, second moment about the horizontal centroidal axis I_xx = 8.5 × 10⁻⁶ m⁴, and a depth of 200 mm. A bending moment M_x = 20 kN·m acts about that axis. Find the maximum direct stress, the radius of curvature of the beam axis, and the anticlastic radius. Answer: σ = M y / I = 2 × 10⁴ × 0.10 / 8.5 × 10⁻⁶ = 235 MPa; R = EI / M = 29.8 m; R′ = R / ν = 90 m.
chapters.trap: Measuring y from an outer surface or a flange instead of the centroidal axis, which shifts the neutral axis and adds a constant to every stress. The other trap is using σ = M y / I when the moment is not about a principal axis — the next chapter shows what happens then.
chapters.prereq: Unit 1 for how a wing or fuselage carries bending; second moment of area from strength of materials.
chapters.leave: Shear flow and shear centre to Unit 5, flange and skin buckling to Unit 6, the unsymmetrical case to chapter 4.2.

chapters.idea: A section with a product second moment I_xy has a neutral axis tilted away from the moment vector, and the stress is a linear function of both x and y.
chapters.depth: Product second moment I_xy = ∫ x y dA, also called the product of inertia of the area, and why a section with an axis of symmetry has I_xy = 0. The general centroidal formula, taking M_x = ∫ σ y dA and M_y = ∫ σ x dA: σ = [(M_y I_xx − M_x I_xy) x + (M_x I_yy − M_y I_xy) y] / (I_xx I_yy − I_xy²). Some syllabi write σ = k₁ x + k₂ y and call the two-constant solution the k method, and some call the same working the neutral axis method. Neutral axis: σ = 0, so tan α = y / x = −k₁ / k₂, measured from the x-axis through the centroid; the moment vector is not perpendicular to the neutral axis unless I_xy = 0. Principal axis method: find the principal directions from Mohr's circle for second moments, centre (I_xx + I_yy)/2 and radius √[((I_xx − I_yy)/2)² + I_xy²], with I_max,min = (I_xx + I_yy)/2 ± that radius; then rotate the moments onto u, v and use σ = (M_u / I_u) v + (M_v / I_v) u with the same sign convention. Always confirm a principal angle by checking that I_uv comes out zero.

figure.aria: Two routes to the same stress field: the general centroidal axes route solves two moment equations and finds the neutral axis, while the principal axes route rotates the moments onto axes where the product second moment vanishes.

chapters.example: A thin-walled section has centroidal second moments I_xx = 5.0 × 10⁻⁶ m⁴, I_yy = 1.2 × 10⁻⁶ m⁴ and I_xy = 0.8 × 10⁻⁶ m⁴. A moment M_x = 5 kN·m acts about the x-axis and M_y = 0. Find the stress at the point x = 50 mm, y = 80 mm, and the angle of the neutral axis. Answer: denominator I_xx I_yy − I_xy² = 5.36 × 10⁻¹²; k₁ = −M_x I_xy / den = −7.46 × 10⁸, k₂ = M_x I_yy / den = 1.12 × 10⁹. σ = −7.46 × 10⁸ × 0.05 + 1.12 × 10⁹ × 0.08 = 52 MPa. tan α = −k₁ / k₂ = 0.667, so the neutral axis is at 33.7° to the x-axis even though the moment is purely about x.
chapters.trap: Reaching for σ = M_x y / I_xx when I_xy is not zero. Also taking x and y from a corner, a web centre line or a boom rather than from the centroid of the section, and dropping the M_y term when the load is skew.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 4.1 for the sign convention and the meaning of I; Mohr's circle for second moments.
chapters.leave: Deflection of the beam to chapter 4.3, shear flow and shear centre to Unit 5.

chapters.idea: Integrate the curvature about each principal axis to get two deflection components, and combine them as vectors — the beam moves perpendicular to the neutral axis, not along the load.
chapters.depth: Curvature about each principal axis, 1/R_u = M_u / (E I_u) and 1/R_v = M_v / (E I_v), and the two-plane deflection components u(z) and v(z) from double integration or from standard beam formulas taken from Unit 2. For a cantilever with a tip load P at angle θ from the u-axis: P_u = P cos θ, P_v = P sin θ, δ_u = P_u L³ / (3 E I_u), δ_v = P_v L³ / (3 E I_v); the resultant is √(δ_u² + δ_v²) at angle tan⁻¹(δ_v / δ_u). State the key result: the deflection direction coincides with the neutral axis direction, so a skew load does not deflect along its own line unless I_u = I_v. Simply supported cases follow from the same two-plane split. Some syllabi add a short MATLAB exercise that plots the deflection shape along the span; the equations do not change.

figure.aria: Two deflection curves for the same cantilever: the component about the strong axis grows to 7.62 mm and the component about the weak axis grows to 22.86 mm, so the weak-axis component dominates the tip movement.

chapters.example: A thin-walled cantilever 2 m long has principal second moments I_u = 4 × 10⁻⁶ m⁴ and I_v = 1 × 10⁻⁶ m⁴, and E = 70 GPa. A tip load of 1 kN acts at 36.9° from the u-axis, so P_u = 800 N and P_v = 600 N. Find the tip deflection in each plane, the resultant, and its direction. Answer: δ_u = 800 × 2³ / (3 × 70 × 10⁹ × 4 × 10⁻⁶) = 7.6 mm; δ_v = 600 × 2³ / (3 × 70 × 10⁹ × 1 × 10⁻⁶) = 22.9 mm; resultant 24.1 mm at 71.6° from the u-axis, while the load is at 36.9°.
chapters.trap: Adding the two components as plain numbers, or drawing the tip deflection along the load line. A skew load on a section with unequal principal second moments deflects at a quite different angle, usually nearer the weak axis.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 4.2 for the neutral axis and the two-plane stress split; Unit 2 for beam deflection formulas.
chapters.leave: Energy methods for complicated or indeterminate beams to Unit 2; thermal curvature to chapter 4.6.

chapters.idea: A thin wall carries direct stress almost uniformly across its thickness, so a real section can be replaced by concentrated boom areas plus wall terms, and I follows by simple summation.
chapters.depth: The thin-walled assumption: wall thickness t much smaller than wall length s, stress taken uniform across t, and the wall carrying shear along its mid-line only. Idealisation into booms (also called stringers or concentrated areas) plus effective walls, and the usual rule that each boom takes half of every wall that meets it. Section properties by summation: A = Σ A_i + Σ t s; I_xx = Σ A_i y_i² + Σ t s³ / 12 for walls running parallel to the x-axis; I_yy likewise; I_xy from the boom coordinates plus the wall terms. Include each wall's own second moment, never count a shared wall twice, and keep units consistent. Open and closed thin-walled sections give the same direct stress — they differ only in shear and torsion, which is Unit 5. State the limits of bending theory: shear lag, local buckling and plasticity make the simple answer optimistic, which is what some syllabi call the applicability of bending theory.

figure.title: Idealising a thin-walled section
figure.aria: The four steps that turn a real stiffened section into boom areas and thin walls, whose summed second moments then feed the bending formula.

chapters.example: A thin-walled rectangular box is 100 mm wide and 60 mm deep, with a uniform wall thickness of 2 mm. Find I_xx and I_yy, then the maximum direct stress for a moment M_x = 2 kN·m. Answer: the two horizontal walls give 2 × (100 × 2) × 30² = 360 000 mm⁴ plus their own 2 × 100 × 2³ / 12 = 133 mm⁴; the two vertical walls give their own 2 × 2 × 60³ / 12 = 72 000 mm⁴. So I_xx = 4.32 × 10⁻⁷ m⁴ and, by the same bookkeeping, I_yy = 6.33 × 10⁻⁷ m⁴. σ = M y / I = 2000 × 0.030 / 4.32 × 10⁻⁷ = 139 MPa.
chapters.trap: Dropping the wall term t s³ / 12 for walls running parallel to the bending axis, and counting a wall that two booms share twice. Mixing millimetres and metres inside I is the other common loss of marks.
chapters.prereq: Chapters 4.1 and 4.2 for how the second moments are used.
chapters.leave: Shear flow, shear centre and Bredt-Batho torsion to Unit 5; local buckling, crippling and effective sheet width to Unit 6.

chapters.idea: Once a wing box is reduced to booms, bending under a skew load is just the unsymmetrical formula applied boom by boom.
chapters.depth: Only a few universities teach this. Take an idealised section with boom areas at known coordinates, find the centroid of the booms alone, compute I_xx, I_yy and I_xy from the boom areas, then apply σ_i = k₁ x_i + k₂ y_i at every boom. Do it first for a symmetric section under a symmetric load, where I_xy = 0 and only M_x survives, then under a skew load where both M_x and M_y act. Repeat for an unsymmetric section: the equations are identical, only I_xy is now non-zero. For a stringer-stiffened wing the input is the bending moment distribution M(z), which comes from Unit 1 — quote it, do not re-derive it. The same steps serve a fuselage frame or a tail plane.

figure.title: Booms: x, y, A, sigma
figure.aria: Four booms of equal area, listed with their x and y coordinates in millimetres and the direct stress each carries under a skew moment, showing that the diagonal pair is most heavily loaded.

chapters.example: A wing box is idealised into four booms of area 200 mm² at (150, 100), (−150, 100), (−150, −100) and (150, −100) mm; all coordinates are in millimetres. It carries M_x = 10 kN·m and M_y = 4 kN·m. Find the stress in each boom. Answer: the boom centroid is the origin, I_xx = 4 × 200 × 100² = 8 × 10⁻⁶ m⁴, I_yy = 4 × 200 × 150² = 1.8 × 10⁻⁵ m⁴, I_xy = 0. With σ = M_x y / I_xx + M_y x / I_yy: boom 1 gets 125 + 33 = 158 MPa, boom 2 gets 125 − 33 = 92 MPa, boom 3 gets −158 MPa, boom 4 gets −92 MPa.
chapters.trap: Taking the centroid of the skin outline instead of the centroid of the boom areas. The skin between booms carries mainly shear, so leaving its area in moves the axis and tilts every stress.
chapters.prereq: Chapters 4.2 and 4.4; Unit 1 for the bending moment distribution along a wing or fuselage.
chapters.leave: Shear flow in tapered and swept wings to Unit 5; panel buckling between stringers to Unit 6.

chapters.idea: A temperature gradient through the depth is a built-in curvature; the beam bends freely, and only restraint turns that curvature into stress.
chapters.depth: Only a few universities teach this. A linear temperature difference gives free thermal strain α ΔT(y). If plane sections stay plane and the beam is free, it curves with 1/R_T = α (ΔT_top − ΔT_bottom) / h and carries no stress at all. Prevent the curvature and a self-equilibrating stress appears: σ(y) = E α [ΔT_mean − ΔT(y)], which is zero at mid-depth for a linear gradient and reaches E α ΔT / 2 at the surfaces, where ΔT is the top-to-bottom difference. Adding axial restraint at both ends superposes the uniform term E α ΔT_mean. Typical aircraft cases: sun on the upper wing skin while the lower skin stays cool, and a hot bleed-air duct running along a fuselage frame. A bimetallic strip is the same calculation with two different α values.

figure.aria: Temperature rises linearly from 5 K at the bottom to 35 K at the top of a 100 mm deep spar, and the stress that appears when curvature is prevented changes sign through mid-depth, reaching about 24 MPa compression at the hot face.

chapters.example: An aluminium spar 100 mm deep has E = 70 GPa and α = 23 × 10⁻⁶ per K. Sun heating makes the top flange 35 °C and the bottom flange 5 °C. Find the free radius of curvature and the stress at the surfaces if the curvature is prevented. Answer: ΔT = 30 K, so 1/R_T = 23 × 10⁻⁶ × 30 / 0.100 = 6.9 × 10⁻³ per m, giving R_T = 145 m. With curvature held, σ = ±E α ΔT / 2 = ±70 × 10⁹ × 23 × 10⁻⁶ × 15 = ±24 MPa, compression on the hot face.
chapters.trap: Applying σ = E α ΔT to a beam that is free to bend. A free beam with a linear gradient bows and stays stress-free; only restraint, whether of curvature or of axial extension, produces stress.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 4.1 for curvature and plane sections; Unit 1 for where the hot and cold surfaces of a wing or fuselage are.
chapters.leave: Thermal stresses in laminates and composites to Unit 6; thermal fatigue and cycling to Unit 3.
